title: Choosing the Right Paint for Kitchens and Bathrooms
seoTitle: Choosing Paint for Kitchens and Bathrooms
seoDescription: Sheen level, mould and mildew resistance and primer: how to choose paint for high-humidity rooms so it resists peeling.
html:
Interior paint comes in a range of formulations, and the wrong one in a high-moisture environment like a kitchen or bathroom creates problems quickly. Understanding the key variables makes the difference between a finish that lasts and one that starts peeling within a year. Choose a satin or semi-gloss sheen, a mildew-resistant formula and the right primer. If you want the painting done for you, send a request through Collingwood Handyman with photos and room sizes. A local service provider can review the request and confirm whether the job is within scope. For prep and application technique, see Interior Painting Tips: How to Get a Professional Finish.

Sheen Level Matters

In high-humidity spaces, use at least a satin or semi-gloss finish. Flat and eggshell paints are porous enough to absorb moisture, which promotes mould growth and makes surfaces difficult to clean. Satin is the minimum for most bathrooms. Semi-gloss is better in areas with direct water contact (around the shower, above the tub).

The tradeoff with higher sheen is that surface imperfections are more visible. Proper prep, such as filling, sanding and priming, is even more important when using semi-gloss.

Mould and Mildew Resistance

Many paint manufacturers offer kitchen and bath specific formulations with built-in mildewcide. These are worth the modest premium in any bathroom that doesn’t have excellent ventilation. However, no paint prevents mould on its own. Adequate ventilation and moisture management are the first line of defence.

For a bathroom with a ventilation fan that runs properly and dries quickly after use, a quality satin-sheen paint with mildewcide additive will last well. For a consistently damp bathroom with poor airflow, address the ventilation issue first, or the best paint in the world will fail prematurely.

Primer in Bathrooms

Use a dedicated primer before painting in bathrooms. Use oil-based primer on areas with staining, or shellac-based primer to seal nicotine, water stains, or heavy odours. A quality primer creates a uniform, adhesion-friendly surface that dramatically extends the life of the finish coat. This step is especially critical during a full bathroom renovation where surfaces have been recently opened up.
